units.title: Unit 01 — What is a collocation?
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 6–7 (PDF pages 10–11).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Learning about collocations · natural word combinations
learningObjectives: Recognise a collocation as a conventional combination of words and distinguish natural from unnatural combinations.
Contrast common partners such as fast/quick, make/do and strong/powerful.
Tell collocations apart from compounds and idioms using examples from the unit.
Use natural combinations in original sentences, noting expressive or more formal alternatives.

items.example: Recognising a collocation helps you choose words that sound natural together.
items.note: A frequent and conventional pairing or group of words, not merely any grammatically possible sequence.

items.example: A fast car passed us on the motorway.
items.note: Fast naturally combines with car; quick car sounds unusual in this sense.

items.example: Fast food is convenient, but I rarely eat it.
items.note: A fixed everyday combination; quick food is not the normal term.

items.example: She took a quick glance at the schedule before the meeting.
items.note: Use quick rather than fast with glance.

items.example: We had a quick meal before catching the train.
items.note: Quick describes the time required; a fast meal is less idiomatic.

items.example: Could you take a photo of the whole team?
items.note: A strong collocation: take is the conventional verb with photo.

items.pt: cumprir as regras; seguir as regras
items.example: Every competitor must keep to the rules.
items.note: Means obey rules; stick to the rules is a common alternative.

items.pt: respeitar as regras; seguir as regras
items.example: Even under pressure, the referee stuck to the rules.
items.note: An accepted alternative to keep to the rules, often emphasising persistence.

items.example: He made an effort to speak clearly during the presentation.
items.note: Use make an effort, not do an effort.

items.example: I usually watch TV after dinner.
items.note: Use watch TV, not look at TV, for the normal activity.

items.example: The truck needs a powerful engine to climb steep roads.
items.note: Powerful is the natural adjective for engine; strong engine is normally not used for this meaning.

items.example: The guide showed us an ancient monument near the river.
items.note: Ancient refers to great age; antique monument is not natural in this context.

items.example: It's normal to make a mistake when learning a new skill.
items.note: Use make, not do, with mistake.

items.pt: atingir 200 km/h; fazer 200 km por hora
items.example: This sports car can do 200 kilometres an hour on a suitable track.
items.note: Do can describe a vehicle travelling at a particular speed; speed figures are contextual, not advice for public roads.

items.example: The word teapot is an example of a compound.
items.note: A unit formed from two or more elements; spelling may be closed, open or hyphenated.

items.example: A good dictionary will explain an idiom as a whole.
items.note: An expression whose meaning is not predictable simply from its individual words.

items.example: There is a small car park behind the station.
items.note: An open compound; primarily British English, corresponding to parking lot in American English.

items.example: The post office closes at five on Fridays.
items.note: An open compound naming a place or service.

items.example: His narrow-minded attitude made discussion difficult.
items.note: A hyphenated compound adjective; it describes unwillingness to consider other views.

items.example: My shoelace came undone during the race.
items.note: A closed compound noun formed from shoe and lace.

items.example: She poured the tea from a small ceramic teapot.
items.note: A closed compound noun, not usually classified as a collocation in this activity.

items.example: I keep the office key on a separate key ring.
items.note: An open compound noun, not the same category as a collocation in the exercise.

items.pt: posto de controle; ponto de inspeção
items.example: Security staff inspected the truck at the checkpoint.
items.note: A closed compound noun.

items.pt: pregar uma peça em alguém; brincar com alguém
items.example: Don't worry; I was only pulling your leg about the promotion.
items.note: An idiom meaning to tease or trick someone playfully; not physical pulling.

items.example: The argument over the seating plan was a storm in a teacup.
items.note: British idiom for exaggerated fuss about a small matter; storm in a teapot is a US variant.

items.example: Smoking is strictly forbidden in the laboratory.
items.note: Strictly intensifies a prohibition; strongly forbidden is unnatural.

items.example: It was bitterly cold outside the mountain shelter.
items.note: An expressive, natural alternative to very cold.

items.example: The corridor was pitch dark during the power cut.
items.note: A fixed, emphatic way to say completely dark.

items.example: The article argues that poverty breeds crime in communities with few opportunities.
items.note: Breed is an expressive verb meaning give rise to; the claim is context-dependent, not a universal fact.

items.example: We ate a substantial meal before the long hike.
items.note: Substantial is more precise than big and often means filling or sizeable.

items.example: I have breakfast at seven before leaving home.
items.note: Have is the usual verb for eating a meal; make breakfast means prepare it.

items.example: My brother offered to make breakfast for everyone.
items.note: A valid alternative in the word-matching activity, but it means prepare breakfast.

items.example: The hikers ate a substantial breakfast before setting off.
items.note: A valid adjective–noun alternative given in the answer key.

items.example: Heavy snow closed the roads overnight.
items.note: Heavy is a natural partner for snow; compare heavy rain.

items.example: You need a valid passport to travel abroad.
items.note: Valid means officially acceptable or still in force.

items.example: The café hosts live music every Saturday.
items.note: Live is pronounced /laɪv/ in this meaning, not /lɪv/.

items.example: She was bitterly disappointed by the cancelled performance.
items.note: Bitterly intensifies disappointment; not the same as simply very sad.

items.example: We need to make a decision before the deadline.
items.note: Use make with decision; do a decision is incorrect.

items.pt: ingressar numa profissão; começar a exercer uma profissão
items.example: After graduation, she decided to take up a profession in healthcare.
items.note: Take up means begin an activity or career; this combination is comparatively formal.

items.example: He learned to play the guitar when he was fourteen.
items.note: Play is used with musical instruments; the is customary here.

items.pt: compor uma música; escrever uma canção
items.example: She wrote a song for her friend's wedding.
items.note: Write is a natural verb with song and songwriting.

items.example: The singer-songwriter performed three new tracks.
items.note: A compound noun for a performer who writes their own songs.

items.example: We made a recording of the rehearsal.
items.note: A natural combination for producing audio or video recordings.

items.pt: estar bastante resfriado; estar com um forte resfriado
items.example: He had a heavy cold and stayed home for two days.
items.note: Heavy cold is natural in British English for a severe cold; heavy modifies the illness.

items.example: The artist sent a demo to a small record company.
items.note: An established noun–noun combination for a music business.

items.example: The actor became famous after appearing in a popular series.
items.note: Become is a natural verb with famous when describing a change in status.

items.example: He hopes to get a job after finishing his course.
items.note: Get a job normally means find or obtain employment.

items.pt: restaurante de comida rápida; lanchonete de fast-food
items.example: They stopped at a fast-food restaurant on the way home.
items.note: A compound adjective modifies restaurant; hyphenation is conventional before the noun.

items.pt: exercer a mesma função; fazer o mesmo trabalho
items.example: We've done the same job for several years.
items.note: Do a job is natural when talking about the work performed.

units.title: Unit 02 — Finding, recording and learning collocations
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 8–9 (PDF pages 12–13).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Learning about collocations · recording and study habits
learningObjectives: Identify useful collocations in reading and dictionary examples, rather than studying isolated words.
Record new combinations in full phrases or original contexts, organising related forms together.
Differentiate make, do, take, have and give in everyday combinations.
Use high-frequency adjective and verb partnerships around pain, study, work, decisions and movement.

items.pt: ir para casa; voltar para casa
items.example: After the conference, they made their way home by bus.
items.note: Make your way means go towards a destination, often through a journey or a crowd.

items.example: My aunt leads an exciting life as a travel photographer.
items.note: Lead a life is a natural verb–noun pattern; the adjective describes its character.

items.example: At times, the training felt difficult, but it was worthwhile.
items.note: An established adverbial expression meaning sometimes.

items.example: He felt desperately jealous of his colleague's success.
items.note: Desperately can intensify an emotional state such as jealous.

items.example: She takes care of her grandfather on weekends.
items.note: A fixed verb phrase for caring for someone or something.

items.example: Her parents got divorced when she was at school.
items.note: Get describes entering a new state; compare be divorced.

items.pt: exigir muito de alguém; fazer exigências a alguém
items.example: The new role makes heavy demands on its manager.
items.note: Make demands on refers to requiring time, effort or resources from someone.

items.pt: ligar para alguém; dar uma ligada
items.example: I'll give you a call once I reach the hotel.
items.note: Informal and common; call someone is a simpler alternative.

items.pt: preparar uma banheira cheia de água; encher a banheira
items.example: She ran a bath after a long day at work.
items.note: Run a bath means fill a bathtub with water, not jog or manage a bath.

items.pt: dor aguda; dor forte e pontual
items.example: He felt a sharp pain in his ankle as he stood up.
items.note: Sharp describes an intense, sudden or clearly localised pain.

items.example: A warm compress helped to ease the pain in her shoulder.
items.note: Ease means reduce pain, not necessarily remove it entirely.

items.example: Slow down before the sharp bend near the bridge.
items.note: Sharp can describe a sudden or tight change of direction.

items.example: The road takes a sharp turn just past the petrol station.
items.note: A sharp turn changes direction abruptly.

items.example: There is a sharp contrast between the two proposals.
items.note: Sharp emphasises a clear and striking difference.

items.example: Researchers noticed a sharp difference between the results.
items.note: Possible with difference, particularly when a clear contrast is meant; marked difference is also common.

items.example: The policy draws a sharp distinction between employees and contractors.
items.note: Sharp distinction emphasises a clear boundary or separation.

items.example: There was a sharp rise in electricity prices last winter.
items.note: Sharp commonly combines with rises in figures and prices.

items.example: The report showed a sharp increase in online sales.
items.note: Near-synonym of a sharp rise, often used with measurable quantities.

items.example: The temperature fell after a sharp drop in wind speed.
items.note: Sharp can emphasise a rapid or sizeable decrease.

items.example: Students have access to the digital library after enrolment.
items.note: A common verb–noun–preposition pattern; access is normally uncountable here.

items.example: She offered me a useful piece of advice before the interview.
items.note: Advice is uncountable; use a piece of advice for one suggestion.

items.pt: encontrar uma maneira; achar uma solução
items.example: We must find a way to test the design without extra equipment.
items.note: A general problem-solving collocation with way.

items.example: Can you find your way to the new office?
items.note: Often means navigate or manage to reach somewhere.

items.pt: aprender da maneira mais difícil; aprender por experiência negativa
items.example: He learned the hard way that backups are essential.
items.note: Means learn from unpleasant experience or mistakes.

items.pt: atrapalhar alguém; ficar no caminho de alguém
items.example: Please move those boxes so they don't get in anyone's way.
items.note: Means obstruct someone physically or interfere with what they want to do.

items.pt: dar preferência ao trânsito; ceder passagem
items.example: Drivers must give way to traffic already on the roundabout.
items.note: A common British-English road expression; yield to traffic is frequent in American English.

items.example: They tried every possible way to contact the supplier.
items.note: Possible commonly combines with way to emphasise available options.

items.example: Make a note of any expressions you hear during the podcast.
items.note: Write something down for future reference; often used as make a note of something.

items.pt: fazer questão de; criar o hábito de
items.example: I make a point of reviewing new expressions every evening.
items.note: Make a point of doing something means deliberately ensure it happens.

items.example: Her family was desperately worried when she missed the flight.
items.note: Desperately intensifies worried, not a physical need for help.

items.example: I plan to enrol on a programming course next month.
items.note: Common in British English; enrol in a course is also acceptable, especially in American English.

items.example: They will make a decision about the contract tomorrow.
items.note: Natural make + decision; do a decision is incorrect.

items.pt: ligar para alguém; dar uma ligada
items.example: Give me a ring when your train arrives.
items.note: An informal British alternative to give someone a call.

items.pt: conversar bastante; ter uma longa conversa
items.example: We had a long chat about our plans over coffee.
items.note: Have a chat is a frequent verb–noun combination.

items.pt: estudar para obter um diploma universitário
items.example: She is studying for a degree in mechanical engineering.
items.note: Study for emphasises working towards a qualification.

items.pt: cumprir os requisitos; atender às exigências
items.example: Applicants must meet the requirements before submitting the form.
items.note: Meet is the natural verb for satisfying conditions or standards.

items.example: The programme prepares students for university entry.
items.note: An established noun–noun combination referring to admission to university.

items.example: He's doing a course in project management this year.
items.note: Common British-English informal expression; take a course is widely used too.

items.pt: abrir uma empresa; montar um negócio
items.example: They hope to set up a business together after graduation.
items.note: Set up means establish or start a business.

items.example: Taking the earlier train was a wise choice.
items.note: Wise suggests sound judgement and good sense.

items.pt: dar uma festa; realizar uma festa
items.example: We're having a party to celebrate her graduation.
items.note: Have a party describes hosting or holding the event, not doing it.

items.pt: dar uma festa; organizar uma festa
items.example: Her colleagues gave a party to celebrate the award.
items.note: An accepted but less common alternative to have or throw a party; the source key includes give a party.

items.pt: fazer uma prova; prestar um exame
items.example: I have to take an exam on Friday.
items.note: Common in British and American English; do an exam is informal and less universal.

items.pt: ministrar uma palestra; dar uma aula expositiva
items.example: The visiting professor will give a lecture on robotics.
items.note: Give a lecture means speak to an audience; take a lecture does not normally mean this.

items.example: Our team has made good progress on the prototype.
items.note: Use make progress, not do progress; progress is uncountable here.

items.example: Everyone must do their duty during an emergency.
items.note: Do your duty means fulfil an obligation.

items.example: We did an exam on the final day of the course.
items.note: Informal British usage recognised in the key; take an exam is more widely suitable.

items.pt: fazer algum trabalho; trabalhar um pouco
items.example: I did some work on the report over the weekend.
items.note: Use do work, not make work, for ordinary tasks.

items.pt: descansar um pouco; fazer uma pausa
items.example: We stopped to have a rest after the hike.
items.note: Have a rest is natural British English; take a rest is possible in some contexts.

items.example: We need to do some shopping before the guests arrive.
items.note: Use do some shopping, not have some shopping.

items.example: He made a special effort to welcome the new employee.
items.note: An expanded version of make an effort; do a special effort is incorrect.

items.example: Could you have a look at my notes?
items.note: A common British-English phrase, often with at.

items.example: Take a look at the diagram before answering.
items.note: A common alternative to have a look.

items.example: The first lesson was very easy for most learners.
items.note: Very naturally modifies easy; totally easy is not idiomatic in the example corrected by the key.

items.example: I found the instructions quite easy to follow.
items.note: Quite easy is natural; its strength may vary by variety and intonation.

items.example: The new interface was extremely easy to learn.
items.note: A stronger natural intensifier; totally easy is awkward here.

items.example: She made a good impression at the interview.
items.note: Use make an impression, not do an impression for this meaning.

items.example: We thoroughly enjoyed the museum visit.
items.note: An adverb–verb combination; utterly enjoyed is unnatural in the corrected example.

items.example: I really enjoyed talking to the new students.
items.note: A common conversational alternative to thoroughly enjoy.

items.example: She was chosen to lead an expedition into the rainforest.
items.note: Lead can mean direct a group or organised activity.

items.example: The moderator will lead a discussion after the talk.
items.note: Lead here means guide a conversation or event.

items.pt: conduzir uma investigação; liderar um inquérito
items.example: A senior official was appointed to lead an inquiry.
items.note: Inquiry commonly means a formal investigation; lead is a natural verb.

items.example: He was desperately ill when the doctors admitted him.
items.note: A strong intensifier, with a serious rather than casual tone.

items.example: I'm desperately busy this week and can't meet before Friday.
items.note: Often used informally for having far too much to do.

items.example: She's desperately keen to join the research team.
items.note: Keen to do something expresses great eagerness, particularly in British English.

items.example: He was desperately in love with a childhood friend.
items.note: An emphatic expression of strong romantic attachment.

items.example: The patient described acute pain in the lower back.
items.note: Acute can refer to severe or sudden pain; it is not simply a synonym for chronic.

items.example: She felt a sudden pain when she lifted the suitcase.
items.note: Sudden describes onset, not necessarily severity.

items.example: The medication helped relieve the pain for several hours.
items.note: Relieve is a natural verb for reducing pain or discomfort.

items.pt: suportar a dor; aguentar a dor
items.example: He had to put up with pain while waiting for treatment.
items.note: Put up with means tolerate something unpleasant.

items.example: Choosing a flexible schedule was a wise decision.
items.note: Wise describes good judgement; compare a wise choice.

items.pt: mais velho e mais sábio; mais experiente
items.example: After several years abroad, she returned older and wiser.
items.note: A familiar expression describing experience and better judgement.

items.pt: sábio depois do ocorrido; fácil falar depois que aconteceu
items.example: It's easy to be wise after the event and criticise the plan now.
items.note: An idiomatic British expression for hindsight.

items.example: Don't be a wise guy when the teacher asks a serious question.
items.note: Informal and often disapproving; it usually means someone who acts too clever.

items.pt: administrar um negócio; gerir uma empresa
items.example: Her parents have run a business for twenty years.
items.note: Run means manage or operate an organisation, not move quickly.

items.example: The trial run went well, and the system now runs smoothly.
items.note: Run smoothly is often used of processes, software, machinery and events.

items.example: Buses run regularly between the airport and the city centre.
items.note: Run describes a transport service operating on a route or schedule.

items.example: She plans to run for political office next year.
items.note: Run for an office means stand as a candidate for election.
